<title>Ibn Bâjja [Avempace]</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/ibn-bajja/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Josep Puig Montada on October 26, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography, notes.html]
 Philosophy in Al-Andalus developed later than in the East; it grew among Muslims and Jews, since both communities were nurtured by a common Arabic. The Muslim community was much larger and it defined the cultural space, a significant part of which was made by Arabic translations of Greek scientifical and philosophical works. <item>
<title>Infinite Regress Arguments</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/infinite-regress/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Ross Cameron on October 26, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography, notes.html]
 An infinite regress is a series of appropriately related elements with a first member but no last member, where each element leads to or generates the next in some sense.[1] An infinite regress argument is an argument that makes appeal to an infinite regress. Usually such arguments take the form of objections to a theory, with the fact that the theory implies an infinite regress being taken to be objectionable....</description>

<item>
<title>Kant’s Transcendental Arguments</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-transcendental/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Derk Pereboom on October 24, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Among Immanuel Kant's (1724 - 1804) most influential contributions to philosophy is his development of the transcendental argument. In Kant's conception, an argument of this kind begins with a compelling premise about our thought, experience, or knowledge, and then reasons to a conclusion that is a substantive and unobvious presupposition and necessary condition of this premise. The crucial steps in this reasoning are claims to the effect that a subconclusion or conclusion is a presupposition and necessary condition of a...</description>

<item>
<title>Locke’s Moral Philosophy</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-moral/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Patricia Sheridan on October 20, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Locke's greatest philosophical work, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, is generally seen as a defining work of seventeenth-century empiricist epistemology and metaphysics. The moral philosophy developed in this work is rarely taken up for critical analysis, considered by many scholars of Locke's thought to be too obscure and confusing to be taken too seriously. The view is not only seen by many commentators as incomplete, but it carries a degree of rationalism that cannot be made consistent with our picture of...</description>

 The organizational form that came to be called "universities" developed over the course of the 11th - 13th centuries in western Europe. <item>
<title>Feminist Social Epistemology</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/feminist-social-epistemology/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Heidi Grasswick on October 16, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Many of the significant contributors to the continually developing field of social epistemology have been feminist epistemologists, theorists who investigate the role of gender and other social identity markers within the practices of knowledge production. Motivated by the political project of eliminating the oppression of women, feminist epistemologists are interested in how the norms and practices of knowledge production both affect the lives of variously situated women and are themselves implicated in multiple systems of oppression....</description>

<item>
<title>Epistemology of Artificial Intelligence</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epistemology-ai/</link>
<description>
[New Entry by Claus Beisbart on October 16, 2026.]
 Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to obtain knowledge and understanding. For example, it is employed to detect objects in images, make predictions, examine mathematical conjectures, and infer causal connections. Indeed, over the last few years, many people have become accustomed to consulting chatbots powered by large language models when they have a question. However, are humans really justified in basing their beliefs on AI outputs? Can they claim to know things based on AI? If so, what is the justification? What kind...</description>

<item>
<title>Feminist Perspectives on Rape</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/feminism-rape/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Rebecca Whisnant on October 15, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Although the proper definition of 'rape' is itself a matter of some dispute, rape is generally understood to involve sexual penetration of a person by force and/or without that person's consent. Rape is committed overwhelmingly by men and boys, usually against women and girls, and sometimes against other men and boys. (For the most part, this entry will assume male perpetrators and female victims.)...</description>

<title>Aristotle’s Categories</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-categories/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Paul Studtmann on October 7, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Aristotle's Categories is a singularly important work of philosophy. It not only presents the backbone of Aristotle's own philosophical theorizing but has exerted an unparalleled influence on the systems of many of the greatest philosophers in the western tradition. <item>
<title>Samuel Alexander</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/alexander/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by Emily A. E. Thomas on October 6, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, Bibliography]
 Australian-born philosopher Samuel Alexander (1859 - 1938) was a prominent figure in early twentieth-century British philosophy. He is best known for advancing "British Emergentism", a movement that held mind "emerges" from matter.  Explanation comes in many forms. <item>
<title>Mill’s Moral and Political Philosophy</title>
<link>https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill-moral-political/</link>
<description>
[Revised entry by David Brink on October 4, 2026. 
Changes to: Main text, notes.html]
 John Stuart Mill (1806 - 1873) was the most famous and influential British philosopher of the nineteenth century. He was one of the last systematic philosophers, making significant contributions in logic, metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, political philosophy, and social theory. He was also an important public figure, articulating the liberal platform, pressing for various liberal reforms, and serving in Parliament. During Mill's lifetime, he was most widely admired for his work in theoretical philosophy and political economy. However,...</description>

<description>
[New Entry by Matt Shafer on October 3, 2026.]
 Friedrich Engels (1820 - 1895) was a preeminent figure in the formation of modern socialist politics and an interdisciplinary autodidact who wrote extensively on history, social theory, natural science, and philosophy.
